questions.stem: What should a candidate do first when attempting a summary question?

options.text: Underline every long sentence in the passage
Read the rubric carefully to establish exactly what is being asked
Count the number of paragraphs in the passage
Copy out the topic sentence of each paragraph

questions.explanation: A summary answer earns nothing unless it answers the question set. The rubric tells you both the subject to search for — for instance "the reasons the writer gives" — and the number of points required, so it controls everything you write afterwards.

distractorRationale.a: Length has no bearing on whether a sentence contains a required point
distractorRationale.c: Counting paragraphs tells you nothing about which points are wanted
distractorRationale.d: Topic sentences are useful later, but only after you know what you are looking for

questions.stem:
Read the extract, then choose the best summary answer.

"Rural clinics fail for reasons that have little to do with money. Drugs arrive but there is no cold chain to keep them usable. Nurses are posted but no accommodation is built for them, so they commute and arrive late. Equipment is delivered but nobody is trained to maintain it."

Rubric: In one sentence, state one reason rural clinics fail.

Which answer is best?

options.text: Drugs arrive but there is no cold chain to keep them usable.
Medicines spoil because the clinics lack the refrigeration needed to store them properly.
Rural clinics fail for reasons that have little to do with money.
There is no cold chain, no accommodation for nurses and no trained maintenance staff.

questions.explanation: Option b gives one reason, in one complete sentence, in the candidate's own words. Option a says the same thing but is lifted verbatim, which earns no marks for expression. Option c repeats the writer's general claim rather than a specific reason, and option d gives three points where one was asked for.

distractorRationale.a: A direct lift from the passage; summary marks require your own words
distractorRationale.c: This is the topic sentence, a general statement rather than one of the reasons
distractorRationale.d: Gives three reasons when the rubric asked for one, so the extra material is ignored or penalised

questions.stem: Why is lifting — copying a whole expression from the passage — penalised in the summary section?

options.text: Because it makes the answer too short
Because it shows no evidence that the candidate has understood the passage
Because examiners cannot read handwriting that copies the printed text
Because the passage is protected by copyright

questions.explanation: The summary section tests comprehension and the ability to re-express ideas concisely. A copied sentence proves only that the candidate can locate words on a page, so the marks for expression cannot be awarded. Rewriting the idea in your own words demonstrates that you have grasped it.

distractorRationale.a: Length is not the issue; a lifted answer may be long or short
distractorRationale.c: Legibility is a separate matter entirely
distractorRationale.d: Copyright plays no part in examination marking

questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"Traffic congestion in Lagos has become self-sustaining. Commuters leave home earlier, which spreads the peak over more hours. Employers respond by relaxing arrival times, which removes any pressure to solve the underlying problem. Last Monday, for instance, a colleague of mine left Ikorodu at half past four in the morning and still reached Marina after nine."

Which sentence is an illustration rather than a main point?

options.text: The first sentence, about congestion becoming self-sustaining
The second sentence, about commuters leaving home earlier
The third sentence, about employers relaxing arrival times
The last sentence, about the colleague who left Ikorodu at half past four

questions.explanation: The phrase *for instance* marks the last sentence as an example supporting the point already made, so it is an illustration. Illustrations, statistics, anecdotes and repetitions are never summary points; only the ideas they support are. Look for signals such as *for instance*, *for example*, *such as* and *in other words*.

distractorRationale.a: This is the writer's central claim and the most important point in the extract
distractorRationale.b: This states one mechanism by which the problem sustains itself, so it is a genuine point
distractorRationale.c: This states a second mechanism and is also a genuine point

questions.stem: A rubric reads: "In three sentences, one for each, state three effects of the flood." Which answer format satisfies the rubric?

options.text: A single long sentence containing all three effects joined by semicolons
Three separate complete sentences, each stating one effect
Three short phrases written as a bulleted list without verbs
One paragraph of five sentences covering the effects and their causes

questions.explanation: The rubric specifies both the number of points and the form, so three separate complete sentences are required — one point per sentence. Marks are awarded per point, and examiners will not hunt through a paragraph or decode a phrase to find them.

distractorRationale.a: Compressing three points into one sentence breaks the stated form
distractorRationale.c: Phrases without finite verbs are not sentences and lose the expression marks
distractorRationale.d: Adds causes that were not asked for and exceeds the number of sentences allowed

questions.stem: A candidate who writes five points when the rubric asks for three improves the chance of scoring full marks.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Examiners mark only the number of points requested, usually taking them in the order written, so the extra points are wasted effort. Worse, a wrong point placed among the first three can displace a correct one and cost a mark outright. Selecting accurately is part of the skill being tested.

questions.stem:
Read the extract, then choose the best summary answer.

"The benefits of learning a second Nigerian language are practical rather than sentimental. A trader who speaks Hausa sells more easily in the North. A nurse who speaks the language of her patients makes fewer diagnostic errors. A civil servant posted across the country settles in faster and is trusted sooner."

Rubric: In one sentence, state the writer's general claim about learning a second Nigerian language.

Which answer is best?

options.text: A trader who speaks Hausa sells more easily in the North.
Learning another Nigerian language brings concrete practical advantages rather than merely emotional ones.
Nurses, traders and civil servants all need to learn a second language.
The benefits of learning a second Nigerian language are practical rather than sentimental.

questions.explanation: The rubric asks for the general claim, and option b states it in the candidate's own words: the gains are practical, not sentimental. Option d is the same idea but lifted word for word, while options a and c offer supporting examples instead of the claim they support.

distractorRationale.a: One of the three illustrations, not the general claim
distractorRationale.c: Lists the people used as examples rather than stating the claim
distractorRationale.d: Correct in content but copied verbatim, so it forfeits the expression marks

questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"The scheme collapsed for one reason above all: nobody owned it. The state saw it as a federal project. The federal officers saw it as a state responsibility. To put the same thing another way, everyone assumed somebody else would pay the running costs."

How many distinct summary points does this extract contain?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

questions.explanation: All four sentences make the same point — that no authority accepted responsibility for the scheme. The two middle sentences illustrate it from each side, and the last is flagged as repetition by *to put the same thing another way*. Recognising restatement is essential, because a candidate who counts each sentence separately wastes three of the points allowed.

distractorRationale.b: Treats the state and federal sentences as two points, though they are two halves of one idea
distractorRationale.c: Counts the illustrations as separate points
distractorRationale.d: Counts every sentence, ignoring the explicit signal of repetition

questions.stem:
Read the extract, then choose the best summary answer.

"Boarding school teaches independence, but it exacts a price. Children learn to manage money, time and disagreement without an adult standing over them. Yet they also lose the daily correction of family life, and some return home strangers to their own parents."

Rubric: In one sentence, state the disadvantage of boarding school mentioned in the passage.

Which answer is best?

options.text: Children learn to manage money, time and disagreement on their own.
Boarding school teaches independence but exacts a price.
Boarders miss the everyday guidance of home life and may become distant from their families.
Boarding school is generally more harmful than beneficial to children.

questions.explanation: The rubric asks specifically for the disadvantage, and option c re-expresses it accurately in the candidate's own words. Option a gives the advantage instead, option b is the lifted topic sentence, and option d states a judgement the passage never makes.

distractorRationale.a: Answers the opposite of the question by giving the advantage
distractorRationale.b: Lifted, and it names the price without saying what the price is
distractorRationale.d: Goes beyond the passage, which weighs both sides without concluding that harm outweighs benefit

questions.stem: Which of the following is acceptable in a summary answer?

options.text: Adding your own opinion about the subject of the passage
Replacing the writer's vocabulary with simpler words of the same meaning
Quoting a full sentence from the passage inside inverted commas
Writing the points as a numbered list of phrases

questions.explanation: Re-expressing the writer's idea in simpler words of your own is exactly what a summary requires, and it is how the expression marks are earned. Personal opinion, quotation and note-form phrases all fall outside the task.

distractorRationale.a: A summary reports the writer's ideas only; your view is irrelevant
distractorRationale.c: Quoting is still lifting, and inverted commas do not rescue it
distractorRationale.d: Points must be written as complete sentences unless the rubric says otherwise
